extracted.intended_audience: Users and developers of PARI/GP (mathematicians, numerical analysts, GP programmers)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and requirements for using PARI/GP special-function and numerical-integration routines (teichmuller, zeta, zetamult, intnum, intnumgauss, etc.), including input constraints, precomputation recommendations, endpoint/decay coding, accuracy caveats, and performance tips.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teichmuller precomputation rule of thumb
rubrics_metrics.description: If more than p / 2 (log2(p) + hammingweight(p)) values of teichmuller are to be computed, then it is worthwhile to initialize a teichmuller table (teichmuller([p,n])) to speed up repeated evaluations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: for p=101, n=100 precomputing T = teichmuller([p,n]) made repetitive teichmuller calls ~21.5× faster (time 1,293 ms vs 60 ms). Use teichmuller(x, T) to exploit cached data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teichmuller tab accuracy vs x precision (caveat)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the accuracy of tab (the argument n in teichmuller([p,n])) is lower than the precision of x, the cached value is not refined to higher accuracy; if the accuracy of tab is larger, then the precision of x is used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: using Tlow = teichmuller([101,2]) then teichmuller(2 + O(101^5), Tlow) yields only limited coefficients; using Thigh with higher accuracy yields full precision. Choose tab precision at least as large as intended x precision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Zeta computation method selection
rubrics_metrics.description: For complex s ≠ 1, ζ(s) is computed using the Euler–Maclaurin summation formula, except when s is an integer: for integer s ≤ 0 or s > 0 even use Bernoulli numbers; for s > 0 odd use modular forms. Power series inputs are allowed for complex s.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: zeta(2) computed via Bernoulli numbers yields Pi^2/6 to precision; zeta(1+x+O(x^3)) returns Laurent expansion. For p-adic s use Kubota–Leopoldt zeta with different rules (power series not allowed). Use suitable method implicitly provided by gzeta(s, prec).

rubrics_metrics.name: p-adic zeta (Kubota–Leopoldt) input restrictions
rubrics_metrics.description: For s a p-adic number, the Kubota–Leopoldt zeta is the unique continuous p-adic function interpolating (1 − p^{−k})ζ(k) at certain negative integers k; power series inputs are not allowed in this case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware you cannot pass power series for p-adic zeta evaluation. To check p-adic values use gzeta(s, prec) and verify interpolation properties (examples provided).

rubrics_metrics.name: zetahurwitz domain constraints and derivative option
rubrics_metrics.description: zetahurwitz(s,x,{der=0}) requires s ≠ 1 and x not a non-positive integer; s may be polynomial, rational, or power series; if der>0 compute the der'th derivative with respect to s.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note derivative with respect to x is simply −s * zetahurwitz(s+1, x). Examples show numerical evaluations and power-series expansions. Use zetahurwitz(GEN s, GEN x, long der, long bitprec).

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple zeta values (zetamult) input constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: zetamult(s) requires s to be a vector of positive integers with s[1] ≥ 2; other formats (evec, index) are accepted as alternate encodings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the bit precision is B, runtime ~ O(k B^2). If provided, T must be output of zetamultinit(w) with w ≥ sum(s_i) to get a small (~10%) speedup. Errors occur when weight > precomputed maxw (e.g., domain error). Use zetamultconvert to move between formats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use zetamultinit precomputation for repeated MZV computations
rubrics_metrics.description: zetamultinit(maxw) initializes inexpensive data to compute multiple zeta values for all weights ≤ maxw and gives a small speedup (typically ~10%) for repeated computations at given accuracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For small weights, zetamultall may be much more efficient. Example: calling zetamultinit(102) yields reasonably small memory even for huge weights. Use T returned from zetamultinit in subsequent zetamult calls.

rubrics_metrics.name: intnum applicability: double-exponential integration assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: intnum uses the double-exponential univariate integration method and assumes the integrand is regular on the integration interval; integrals with singularities must be split into subintegrals where the function has no singularities except possibly at endpoints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Polynomials in logarithms are not considered singular; singularities considered are algebraic (asymptotic to C(x − a)^−α with α > −1) or simple derivative discontinuities. Split integrals around singularities (example: handle abs(x) singularity at 0).

rubrics_metrics.name: intnum tab argument and precomputation
rubrics_metrics.description: The tab argument to intnum can be (i) a non-negative integer m to multiply sampling points by 2^m, or (ii) a precomputed integration table from intnuminit to skip an O(D log D) precomputation step and speed up repeated/inner integrations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using intnuminit is particularly useful for multivariate integrals where many internal integrations share the same structure; increasing m increases runtime roughly by factor 2^m. Try increasing m until consecutive results agree within desired tolerance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specifying endpoint behavior in intnum (finite endpoints)
rubrics_metrics.description: For finite endpoint a, coding as [a, α] means the integrand has a singularity of the form (x − a)^α up to logarithms; if α ≥ 0 the function is assumed regular.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using a wrong singularity exponent degrades accuracy. Example: intnum(x=[0,c],1,x^c) can restore full accuracy when c = -9/10. Choose α carefully; if omitted default regularity is assumed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specifying endpoint behavior in intnum (infinite endpoints & decay/oscillation coding)
rubrics_metrics.description: [±oo, α] encodes asymptotic behavior at infinity: α = 0 (or omitted) assumes moderate decay (at least O(x^{-2}) but not exponential); α > 0 assumes exponential decay roughly exp(−α x); α < −1 assumes slow polynomial decay x^{α} and requires sharp α; α = k * I encodes oscillation like cos(kx)g(x) and α = −k * I encodes sin(kx)g(x).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is critical to supply exact k for oscillatory coding. If integrand is product of exponential decay and oscillation you may choose either coding: choose [±oo, α] if exponential dominates, otherwise [±oo, k*I]. Examples show wrong choice yields nonsense while correct choice gives high precision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power-series endpoints and valuation restriction
rubrics_metrics.description: Endpoints a and b may be power series of non-negative valuation, giving a power-series expansion for the integral, but the valuation cannot be negative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Polynomials and rational functions are converted to power series using current seriesprecision. intnum fails if integral is singular with constant coefficient of the series as limit; in that case use explicit [limit, exponent] coding and only integer tab (not precomputed table).

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling apparent singularities
rubrics_metrics.description: Apparent singularities may often be ignored but can cause enormous local loss of accuracy; remedy by defining the function differently near special points (e.g., using a Taylor expansion) and using a piecewise definition with thresholds chosen by the user.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: f(x)=1/(exp(x)-1)-exp(-x)/x is numerically dangerous near 0; create F = truncate(f(t+O(t^10))) and define g(x)=if(x>1e-18,f(x),subst(F,t,x)). The user must choose cutoff constants appropriately (e.g., 10^-18).

rubrics_metrics.name: True singularities require explicit exponent coding
rubrics_metrics.description: For true singularities at endpoints, providing the endpoint as [a, α] with correct α yields accurate results; omitting or giving wrong α degrades accuracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: intnum(x=[0,-1/2],1,x^(-1/2)) gives full precision while naive intnum without coding yields far fewer correct decimals. Use exact exponents for true singularities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oscillating integrands: linearization and exact k requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: For oscillating integrals, it is often necessary to linearize trigonometric polynomials and express as sum of pure cos(kx) or sin(kx) terms to use [±oo, k*I] coding; otherwise results will be nonsense unless exact k is provided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: sin(x)^3 must be expanded as (3*sin(x)-sin(3*x))/4 to use correct k values. Using incorrect k yields large errors; splitting into several oscillatory integrals with correct k values or change of variables can fix the issue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Warning about divergent integrals
rubrics_metrics.description: intnum may assign a reasonable value to diverging integrals; such values should be used at your own risk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: intnum(x = 0, [oo, -I], x^2*sin(x)) produced a finite-looking value that corresponds to analytic continuation rather than an absolutely convergent integral. Do not rely blindly on outputs for divergent cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multivariate integration performance advice
rubrics_metrics.description: For multivariate integrals, use successive univariate integration and precompute intnuminit tables for internal integrations; precomputing tab for inner integrals gives significant speedups because the internal integral matters most.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: computing double integral on unit disc: using tab = intnuminit(-1,1) and passing tab to inner intnum reduced time from ~3,092 ms to ~252 ms. Precompute when doing many inner integrations at same precision and interval type.

rubrics_metrics.name: intnumgauss usage and tab option
rubrics_metrics.description: intnumgauss performs Gauss–Legendre quadrature on a compact interval [a,b]; tab may be omitted, precomputed with intnumgaussinit, or given as integer n to call intnumgaussinit(n) and use n-point quadrature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Testing examples show accuracy improves with n; however, for large intervals it's better to split and change variables rather than drastically increase n. Use intnumgaussinit to precompute nodes/weights.

rubrics_metrics.name: intnumgaussinit default n and error growth with interval length
rubrics_metrics.description: intnumgaussinit(n) initializes n-point Gauss–Legendre tables; if n is omitted, default n ≈ realprecision is chosen, suitable for analytic functions on [-1,1]. Error bound depends exponentially on n and on interval length, so n should increase with interval length.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Error bounded by ((b-a)^{2n+1} (n!)^4 f^{(2n)}(ξ)) / ((2n+1)[(2n)!]^3). Recommendation: split the integral and change variables rather than increasing n too much for long intervals.

rubrics_metrics.name: intnuminit encoding of interval behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: intnuminit(a,b,{m=0}) initializes tables describing compactness, singularities at endpoints, speed of decrease, or oscillations at infinity for integration from a to b; order of endpoints matters when exponents are specified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: intnuminit returns internal parameters [h, x0, w0, xp, wp, xm, wm] used by intnum (step h, φ(0), φ'(0), sampled φ(nh) and φ'(nh) values). If m present, multiply default sampling points by 2^m. Note equivalences: intnuminit(-1,1) == intnuminit(0,Pi); but intnuminit([0,-1/2],[1,-1/3]) is not symmetric — order matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: intnumromb suitability and flags
rubrics_metrics.description: intnumromb (Romberg integration) is suitable for low-to-moderate accuracy and very regular functions; flags control behavior: flag=0 default for smooth functions on bounded intervals; flag=1 general slow driver; flag=2 tailored for infinite endpoints using t=1/x change (requires ab>0); flag=3 allows integrand undefined at an endpoint (one-sided continuity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not require too much accuracy (≈30 decimal digits is reasonable). Perform analytic cleanup to remove singularities; for improper integrals ensure sufficient decay. Representing infinity by a large finite number is okay but watch for underflow with rapidly decreasing functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: laurentseries domain requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: laurentseries(f,{M},{x}) expands f as a Laurent series around x=0 to order M; it requires the ability to evaluate f on a power series with zero constant term (series valuation = 0).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If series valuation != 0, laurentseries fails (domain error). Individual Laurent coefficients can be retrieved from the result with polcoeff; laurentseries is faster and often more precise than repeated derivnum calls for series coefficients.

rubrics_metrics.name: asympnum heuristic algorithm and alpha handling
rubrics_metrics.description: asympnum(expr,{k=20},{alpha=1}) attempts a heuristic asymptotic expansion assuming u(n) ≈ Σ a_i n^{−iα}; the algorithm is heuristic, performs repeated calls to limitnum, and may fail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If alpha is non-integer expect loss of accuracy; precompute alpha to double accuracy where needed. Normalizing by a limit computed to high precision often improves term extraction (example: Stirling expansion). Use asympnum0 when passing a precomputed vector.

rubrics_metrics.name: limitnum requirements and vector/closure guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: limitnum(expr,{k=20},{alpha=1}) performs Lagrange–Zagier numerical extrapolation to estimate limits of sequences; if given a vector it must be long enough (at least k times realprecision), otherwise prefer a closure n->u(n); extrapolating from u(kn) for k>1 may improve results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When vector is too short limitnum errors (non-existent component). Examples show using vectors of size matching precision and sub-sampling (u(10*n)) yields better accuracy. limitnum is heuristic and depends on assumed asymptotic form.

rubrics_metrics.name: derivnum behavior depending on evaluation point type
rubrics_metrics.description: derivnum(X=a, expr, {ind=1}) performs numerical differentiation: when a is a numerical type perform numerical derivation; when a is a polynomial or power series compute derivatives via series substitution; ind may be integer m to return f^{(m)}(x) or a vector of orders to return multiple derivatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples show derivnum on series and high-order derivatives; for high-order derivatives or many derivative evaluations laurentseries may be faster/more precise. Library variants accept function pointers for use in compiled code.
